20250620200355.an:
The pilot and the passenger were attempting to take off when surveillance video captured, and a witness heard, the sound of the airplane’s engine backfiring followed by a sudden decrease and increase in engine power. Dark smoke was also seen trailing under the belly of the airplane. Data downloaded from the airplane’s onboard engine monitor recorded an rpm drop from 2,600 to 1,500 rpm then back to 2,500 rpm shortly after the airplane became airborne. Fuel flow, manifold pressure, and horsepower readings uniformly tracked with the decrease/increase of rpm, consistent with the pilot quickly reducing the throttle to idle then back to full power. During the takeoff, the pilot advised the air traffic controller that the airplane was having an engine problem and that he planned to “head up and turn back.” The airplane subsequently made a right turn toward the intersecting runway shortly after the engine backfired and it’s possible the pilot reduced power in an attempt to land but changed his mind and decided to circle back to another runway. The airplane then entered a steep left turn and descended, in what a witness described as a stall-like state. The last radar return indicated the airplane was about 110 ft above the ground at a groundspeed near its published stall speed. According to data downloaded from the airplane’s engine monitor, the engine was operating near full power as the airplane descended to ground contact.
Postaccident examination of the engine revealed the No. 2 cylinder bottom spark plug was loose, and stains/residue from combustion exhaust gas leakage was visible around the spark plug port consistent that it had been loose prior to the accident. Review of the airplane’s engine maintenance logbook revealed that the spark plugs were, “cleaned, gapped, tested, and rotated” at the last annual inspection, about 37 hours before the accident. There were no other entries in the engine maintenance logbook regarding removal of the spark plugs after the annual inspection. According to the engine manufacturer’s service instruction on how to install spark plugs, the spark plugs should have been torqued to a specific torque value to prevent them from coming loose. 
Examination of the fuel system and its components revealed evidence of water/corrosion and debris; however, testing found no indication that would have precluded fuel from reaching the engine. While the data showed that the cylinder head temperature was low on the No. 1 cylinder, there was no evidence of a stuck valve, and the ignition system tested normally. An erratic exhaust gas temperature (EGT) reading for the No. 1 cylinder was also recorded for the entire flight. The EGT data had been erratic since the engine’s last annual inspection. The No.1 cylinder’s EGT connector was found undamaged and the yellow (positive) wire for the EGT probe was not connected (the red wire was connected). As such, the probe had most likely not been working properly since the last annual inspection.

HISTORY OF FLIGHTOn June 19, 2025, at 0847 eastern daylight time, a Mooney M20F, N9573M, was involved in an accident near Beverly, Massachusetts. The commercial pilot/owner and the passenger were fatally injured. The flight was conducted as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
A review of air traffic control tower communications and radar data provided by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) revealed the airplane was cleared for takeoff at 0845 from runway 16 at Beverly Municipal Airport (BVY), Beverly, Massachusetts. According to the tower controller on duty, when the airplane was about 500 ft above the runway, he observed dark smoke trailing under the belly of the airplane. The controller asked the pilot if everything was okay and cleared him to land on any runway. The pilot responded he was having engine trouble, and they were going to “head up and turn back.” The controller cleared the pilot to land on runway 09. The control said the airplane initially turned right toward runway 09, then turned left. The airplane continued banking to the left into a steeper turn and descended behind trees.
A witness, who was a flight instructor at BVY, watched the airplane depart. He said there was a “significant reduction in power” when the airplane reached 150 ft agl and was about halfway down the 5,001-ft-long runway. He said, “A few seconds later it seemed as though the engine got power back partially. The pilot initiated a left turn to the east.” While turning the engine sounded as though there was another significant reduction in power. The airplane then began to descend with its wings level eventually in what appeared to be a “stalled” state behind the tree line to the accident site.
Airport security video captured the airplane shortly after it became airborne, and dark smoke could be seen trailing under the airplane. The video, which had no sound, showed the airplane initially turning to the right before it turned left. The airplane then entered a steep turn and descended behind trees.
Another surveilence camera located at the airport captured the sound of the airplane as it was departing and the last few moments of the flight before impact. About 0846:28, the sound of the airplane taking off was heard followed by the sound of the engine backfiring at 1846:32. The sound of engine power then quickly decreased before a suddenly increase. The airplane appeared to continue to climb with the engine running before it entered a very steep left turn to the northeast. The airplane descended and disappeared behind trees. 
The last radar return received on the airplane was at 0846:55. At that time, the airplane was 217 ft mean sea level (110 ft above ground level) at a ground speed of 65 knots (see figure 1).

Figure 1 - The airplane’s final two radar-derived positions with the wreckage location/accident site annotated. PERSONNEL INFORMATIONThe pilot held a commercial pilot certificate with ratings for airplane single-engine land and instrument airplane. His most-recent FAA second-class medical certificate was issued on September 2, 2020, without limitations. A review of the pilot’s logbook revealed that his last logged flight was on April 4, 2025. At that time, he had logged 429 total flight hours of which, 77.2 hours were in the accident airplane. AIRCRAFT INFORMATIONThe airplane’s last annual inspection of the engine was completed on October 11, 2024, about 37 hours prior to the accident. At the time of the accident, the engine had accrued a total of 2,268.9 hours and 553.7 hours since overhaul. 
A laminated Emergency Checklist was found in the wreckage. According to the checklist, the first item listed after losing engine power immediately after takeoff was to maintain an airspeed of 100 miles per hour (mph) or 87 knots indicated airspeed.
According to the airplane’s owner’s manual, the stall speed of the airplane with 15 degree of flaps extended (takeoff flap setting) in wings level flight (0-degree bank) and landing gear retracted was 64 mph or approximately 55 knots. The stall speed rose to roughly 93 mph (approx. 80 knots) in a 60° bank. At the time of the accident, the engine had accrued a total of 2,268.9 hours and 553.7 hours since overhaul.

According to the airplane’s owner’s manual, the stall speed of the airplane with 15 degree of flaps extended (takeoff flap setting) in wings level flight (0-degree bank) and landing gear retracted was 64 mph or approximately 55 knots. The stall speed rose to roughly 93 mph (approx. 80 knots) in a 60° bank. WRECKAGE AND IMPACT INFORMATIONThe airplane impacted a grass berm adjacent to a two-lane road with the left wing, then crossed the road and impacted a light pole where it came to rest upright and perpendicular to the road. There was no postimpact fire. The left wing separated from the airframe and was found about 15 to 20 ft forward and to the right of the main wreckage. The wing tip, aileron, and flap had separated, and the fuel tank was breached; however, when the fuel tank cap was removed, fuel was observed about 3-inches below the tab. The tail section separated from the airframe and came to rest to the left of the fuselage. The engine and propeller assembly remained partially attached to the firewall and was displaced about 70 degrees to the left. The right wing (including the aileron and flap) remained secure to its respective wing root. The right flap appeared to be extended about 15 degrees (takeoff setting), and the landing gear were retracted. The right wing fuel tank was not breached and about 32 gallons of 100LL were visually observed when the fuel tank cap was removed.
The airplane’s flight control tubes were fractured in several locations due to impact; however, continuity was established for all major flight controls to the cockpit area. 
The airplane was equipped with two Electronics International engine monitors; however, only one monitor recorded the accident flight. Data downloaded from the monitor revealed that during the last 25 seconds of the flight, the engine rpm dropped from 2,600 to 1,500 before it increased back to 2,600 and settled at 2,500 rpm. Fuel flow, manifold pressure and engine-horsepower readings all uniformly followed the decrease and increase of rpm. Just before the data ended, there was another small reduction/increase in fuel flow and rpm that coincided with an increase in the No. 2 thru 4-cylinder exhaust gas (EGT) temperatures.
The data also indicated that the No. 1 cylinder EGT reading was erratic for the entire accident flight and had been erratic since the date of the last annual inspection in October 2024. Examination of photos taken of the No. 1 cylinder at the accident site revealed the OLC-2 connector for the K-type EGT probe was not damaged. However, the yellow (positive) wire was disconnected from the connector, and the red (negative) wire was connected. The yellow wire not being connected would result in erratic EGT readings.
The engine was separated from the airframe for examination. The top spark plugs were removed from the engine, and the plugs appeared dark in color. The engine’s crankshaft rotated freely via manual rotation of the propeller, and compression/valve train continuity were established on each cylinder. The compression was low on the No. 2 cylinder compared to the other cylinders. The engine sustained impact damage and the No. 2 cylinder intake tube had been pushed into the No. 2 cylinder bottom spark plug. The spark plug exhibited a slight bend. 
Further examination revealed that the No. 2 bottom spark plug was loose and the area around the plug port exhibited dark combustion exhaust leakage as evidence by staining/residue on the exterior and cooling fins, consistent with the plug being loose at the time of impact (figure 2). The spark plug’s position was marked and when it was manually moved to a hand tight position (or zero-torque position), it took about 1/8th to 1/4 - inch turn to do so. When it was attempted to tighten the spark plug to facilitate better compression, the plug broke at the base of the threaded section that housed the electrodes as soon as torque was applied. The broken spark plug was examined by the NTSB Materials Laboratory, and the fracture surfaces were consistent with overstress. No preexisting anomalies were identified. The No. 2 cylinder top sparkplug was installed in the bottom port, and a another compression test was performed. The compression was consistent with the other cylinders.

Figure 2 - Combustion exhaust leakage stains and residue around the No. 2 cylinder bottom spark plug port.
Review of the airplane’s engine maintenance logbook revealed that the spark plugs were, “cleaned, gapped, tested, and rotated” at the last annual inspection in October 2024. There were no other entries in the engine maintenance logbook regarding the removal of the sparkplugs after the annual inspection.
According to Lycoming Service Instruction 1042AH, which was active at the time of the accident, Spark Plug Installation Guidelines, the installation torque values were:
All spark plugs - 420 in.-lbs. (or 35 ft.-lbs.) (47.5 Nm)
5/8-24 (16 mm-24) lead nuts - 80 to 90 in.-lbs. (9 to 10 Nm)
3/4-20 (19 mm-20) lead nuts - 110 to 120 in.-lbs. (12 to 13.6 Nm)
The magnetos remained secured in the accessory housing. A timing check was performed; the left magneto timing was late, near top dead center. The left magneto flange was fractured and appeared to have shifted during the impact sequence. The magneto was removed, the drive was secure, and it sparked from all four posts when the impulse coupling was snapped by hand. 
The right magneto was secure to the engine and was correctly timed. The magneto was removed, the drive was secure, and spark was observed from all four posts when the drive was rotated with a drill.
The fuel selector was found on the right-wing fuel tank. When the selector was moved by hand, it moved freely to the “left” and “off” detents. The firewall fuel strainer was removed, and a small amount of debris and water were in the bowl. A few strings of unidentified debris were on the screen.
Per the M20F Owner’s Manual, the electric boost pump was to be turned on for takeoff; however, the toggle switch on the instrument panel was found in the off position. During the postaccident examination, when power was applied to the pump, and the pump motor operated. 
The fuel line from the boost pump to the main fuel supply line to the engine was breached from impact. When compressed air was blown through the main fuel line at each wing root, fuel sprayed out of the lines at the fuel selector strainer indicating that fuel was capable of reaching the fuel selector from both tanks. The breached fuel lines and the main fuel supply line to the engine were also clear of debris. 
The fuel injector servo was removed from the engine, and clear 100LL fuel was drained from the servo body. The fuel screen was removed and absent of debris. The fuel manifold was removed along with the fuel injectors. When the No. 3 fuel injector was removed, the insert separated. The injector and insert were clear of debris. All of the other injectors/inserts were clear of debris. The manifold was disassembled, and fuel was in the manifold body. The fuel was absent of debris/water and the diaphragm was intact. 
The fuel servo and manifold were removed and sent out to the manufacturer to be bench tested. A small amount of water, corrosion and sand-like debris were found in the servo; however, the servo and manifold/injectors tested to manufacturer specifications. 
The fuel pump remained secured to the engines accessory housing. The fuel pump was removed, and fuel was present in the fuel pump. It created pressure, and suction when the lever was actuated. The pump was disassembled and a white sealant-like material was observed in the fuel outlet chamber and pump chamber. Evidence of corrosion was also observed in both chambers. 
The oil filter adapter broke from engine due to impact, and the back of engine was covered with oil. The filter was absent any metallic debris. The oil sump screen was removed and absent of any debris. 
The air filter was clean.
The engine monitor also indicated that the cylinder head temperature (CHT) for the No. 1 cylinder had a consistent low temperature reading for the entire flight of about 275 degrees F. A lighted borescope was used to examine the interior of the No. 1 cylinder, and no evidence of a stuck valve was observed. The cylinder’s valve guide was measured using a Lycoming valve gage guide (R-ST-310). The test indicated the valve’s play was tight and below minimums per Lycoming Service Bulletin 388. The No. 1 cylinder was then removed from the engine along with the remaining cylinders for comparison.
The interior walls of the No. 1, 2, and 3 cylinders exhibited some lead bromide deposits. The interior walls of the No. 4 cylinder appeared new (replaced at the last annual) and did not exhibit any lead bromide deposits.
The exhaust valve was removed from the No. 1 cylinder. The valve was easily removed from the cylinder, and no deposits were observed on the valve stem. No mechanical deficiencies or malfunctions were observed that would have contributed to the low CHT reading. MEDICAL AND PATHOLOGICAL INFORMATIONAn autopsy was conducted on the pilot by the Commonwealth of Massachusetts, Office of the Chief Medical Examiner on July 20, 2025. The cause of death was determined to be multiple blunt force injuries as the manner of death to be an accident.
Toxicology testing performed at the FAA Forensic Sciences Laboratory identified Minoxidil in the pilot’s urine. Minoxidil is a medication commonly used to stimulate hair growth.

American Airlines flight 1286 (AAL1286) encountered unexpected convectively induced turbulence (CIT) while at 25,000 ft (FL250) about 17 minutes after departure from Miami International Airport (MIA), Miami, Florida. One flight attendant (FA) received a serious injury, and 3 FAs and 6 passengers received minor injuries. The seatbelt sign was illuminated at the time of the event. No significant convective weather or turbulence was forecasted or depicted during the flight crew’s flight planning or displayed on the onboard weather radar, or WSI weather app before the event. 
At the time of the event, multiple FAs were conducting cabin service with beverage carts positioned in the aisle, and one passenger was occupying the aft lavatory. The turbulence lasted about 5 to 8 seconds and consisted of abrupt vertical accelerations, resulting in multiple FAs being thrown to the floor or striking interior cabin structures, unsecured service items becoming airborne, and damage to the aft lavatory door.
AAL1286 flight crew indicated they had the airborne radar tilt up to 3.5 degrees during the period and likely scanned over the area. Airborne radar does not detect echoes less than 20 dBZ, while echoes of 45 dBZ were detected under the flight track. The model High-Resolution Rapid Refresh (HRRR) sounding indicated a potential for updrafts to 144 knots or 4,173 fpm, and an unstable atmosphere. 
Following the turbulence encounter, the captain transferred control to the first officer and communicated with the cabin crew to assess injuries. A deadheading captain assisted with cabin coordination and injury assessment. The flight crew contacted dispatch and MedLink and declared an emergency with air traffic control. Based on medical guidance and aircraft position, the decision was made to continue to Raleigh-Durham International Airport (RDU), North Carolina. The airplane landed without further incident. Emergency medical personnel met the flight upon arrival at RDU, and injured crew members and at least one passenger were transported to local hospitals for evaluation and treatment. One FA was diagnosed with a fracture to her arm.
A review of the weather conditions indicated that there were no frontal boundaries over the area and no organized jet streams or strong winds aloft to indicate any potential clear air turbulence (CAT). While the NWS convective outlook expected a widely scattered area of general thunderstorms over Florida and the surrounding coastal waters during the time period. The High-level Significant Weather Prognostic Chart indicated no organized areas of convection or turbulence over the general route of flight, and no PIREPs or inflight weather advisories for thunderstorms or turbulence were current at the time of the turbulence encounter. 
A review of the NWS weather surveillance radar 1988 doppler (WSR88D) and satellite imagery showed an area of scattered echoes over central Florida and off the Florida coast between the Bahamas Islands. A review of the flight path confirmed that the flight over flew an area of developing echoes near 45 dBZ which rapidly increased in height between FL250 to FL420 surrounding the period, while the GOES-19 infrared image indicated radiative cloud tops near FL380 at the time of the turbulence encounter. Several cloud-to-ground lightning strikes were noted with the echoes after the flight had overflown the area of echoes. Thus, other than the flight’s airborne weather radar no visual clues were available prior to the encounter.
A HRRR numerical model indicated an unstable atmosphere with potential strong updrafts or maximum vertical velocities (MVV) near to 14,173 fpm. The Eddy Dissipation Rate (EDR) recorded by the accident flight was 0.665 which corresponded to the upper bounds of severe turbulence for a medium weight category aircraft. 
A review of the astronomical conditions indicated that official nighttime conditions existed at the time of the encounter with no illumination from the Moon, which was more than 30 degrees below the horizon at the time of the encounter.

The pilot was returning to his home-base airport after some minor maintenance to the airplane’s emergency locator transmitter. The preflight checks and run-up were normal and he performed a short-field takeoff from a 2,895-ft-long turf runway. As the airplane lifted off and began to climb, engine power decreased. The pilot ensured that the throttle and mixture controls were full forward, but the engine only retained partial power and he was unable to maintain altitude. The pilot subsequently landed the airplane hard on level terrain off the airport property, collapsing the landing gear and resulting in substantial damage to the airframe and right wing.
Postaccident examination of the engine revealed that the throttle cable sleeve had separated from a connection where it was crimped to secure it. Forward movement of the throttle would result in the cable forming a “U” shape and remaining slack. With the throttle in this position, the engine was likely unable to produce sufficient power to continue the climb. The examination identified no other evidence of a mechanical malfunction or failure that would have precluded normal operation.
Although the engine had been overhauled and reinstalled about a year before the accident, review of maintenance records showed no documentation that a new throttle cable assembly was installed, nor was it required to be. The preexisting engine throttle cable was reattached after the overhaul, inspected, and exercised with no anomalies observed. Additionally, no maintenance to the throttle controls had been documented in the logs between the time of the engine overhaul and the accident. Given the available information, it is likely that the single crimp holding the throttle sleeve in place became loose and detached, which resulted in the throttle moving to a low power position and did not allow the pilot to control the throttle after it separated.

On June 23, 2025, about 0935 eastern daylight time, a Cessna R182 airplane, N262AL, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Milton, Florida. The airline transport pilot and pilot-rated passenger were not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 positioning flight.
The pilot departed from Dothan Regional Airport (DHN), Dothan, Alabama, and flew to J22 Ranch Airport (16FL), Milton, Florida, to have a new emergency locator transmitter battery installed. About 90 minutes after arriving, the maintenance was completed, and the pilot departed for the flight back to DHN. The pilot reported that he conducted preflight checks and a run-up, then performed a short-field takeoff from runway 36, a 2,895-ft turf runway. After the takeoff roll and rotation, the pilot began the initial climb and retracted the landing gear. The airplane was about 100 ft over the runway when the engine started losing power. The pilot stated that the engine retained partial power, but that it was not enough to maintain altitude.
The pilot attempted to troubleshoot the loss of engine power; he checked to make sure the throttle and mixture were full forward, but was unable to regain full power. The pilot subsequently landed off the departure end of the runway and slightly east of the centerline. During the final approach, he held the nose up and landed hard on the level terrain. The impact collapsed the right main landing gear and the airplane skidded to a stop, resulting in substantial damage to the airframe. 
Postaccident examination of the airplane revealed that the right wing tip was crushed upward, and there was buckling of the wings and fuselage. The 3-blade metal propeller was slightly curled on the outer 12 inches of the blades. The pilot reported that there were 65 gallons of 100LL aviation fuel on board at takeoff.
During a subsequent engine examination, the engine crankshaft was manually rotated by the propeller, which confirmed continuity of the powertrain. Thumb compression and suction were achieved on all cylinders. The magnetos sparked on all leads when the input drives were rotated. A lighted boroscope was used to examine all 6 cylinders; no anomalies were observed. During a functional check of the throttle, mixture, and propeller controls, it was revealed that the throttle control end had pulled out of the plunger guide. Manual operation of the throttle did not activate full throttle control to the engine. There was about a 2 1/2 -inch detachment of the throttle plunger and cable where the unit was separated. The line was slack when the throttle was moved to the full power setting, which would have resulted in the engine in a partial power condition (see figure). 

Figure - Throttle control end and plunger diagram from illustrated parts catalog and photograph of detached throttle cable and plunger. Note the single crimp at the yellow arrow and the area where it should be secured. Yellow circles identify parts affected. 
A review of maintenance records revealed that on October 3, 2022, the engine was removed for overhaul. This included the installation of an overhauled Marvel-Schebler carburetor 10-5235 (Model HA-6). The zero-timed engine was reinstalled, along with magnetos, a new starter and fuel pump. There was no replacement of the throttle cable assembly during reinstallation on March 21, 2024. A subsequent engine run and break-in revealed no defects, and the records indicated that no further maintenance related to the throttle was performed before the accident. A mechanic with inspection authorization who worked on the airframe after the overhauled engine was reinstalled stated that the throttle cable assembly was reconnected to the engine. The subsequent inspection included a visual inspection of the cable controls to ensure proper and secured rigging followed by an exercise of the system; it was manually actuated through the throttle to ensure there was no binding and smooth operation.

The sport pilot of the gyroplane reported that he intended to complete two airport traffic pattern circuits over a runway. He planned to conclude the first circuit with a low approach over the runway and the second circuit with a full stop landing. The majority of the first circuit was uneventful; however, about halfway down the 4,001-ft-long runway during the low approach, when the pilot applied full throttle to climb, the gyroplane did not respond as he had expected. He then pitched forward to increase airspeed and rotor speed, but the gyroplane still would not climb. As his altitude became lower, the pilot decided to perform a forced landing to a grass area beyond the runway, during which the gyroplane’s empennage and main rotor were substantially damaged. 

Following the accident, the pilot stated that he was not sure if the engine was unable to produce full power, or if he allowed the gyroplane to “fall behind the power curve” as he was distracted looking for traffic utilizing a crossing runway. Data download from the gyroplane’s primary flight display, engine management system, and engine control unit were reviewed following the accident. The data did not reveal evidence of any preimpact mechanical malfunctions or failures and showed that just prior to the pilot terminating the climb attempt, the engine rpm was increasing while the rotor rpm was decreasing, consistent with the pilot’s statement that he may have let gyroplane get “behind the power curve”. During the impact sequence, there was a sudden increased in throttle position along with a rapid spike in engine rpm, beyond its maximum rated speed, likely due to the propeller blades shearing off and unloading resistance on the engine.

On June 23, 2025, about 0955 eastern daylight time, an experimental amateur-built Gyro Technic GT-VX2 gyroplane, N62XF, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Swansea, New Hampshire. The sport pilot sustained minor injuries. The gyroplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
 
The sport pilot reported that he intended to complete two airport traffic pattern circuits on runway 32 at Dillan/Hopkins Airport (EEN), Keene, New Hampshire. He planned to conclude the first circuit with a low approach over the runway and the second circuit with a full stop landing. The first circuit was uneventful. During the low approach, while the gyroplane was near the mid-point of the 4,001-ft-long runway, about 50 ft above the runway, and at an airspeed about 50 mph, the pilot applied full throttle, but the gyroplane would not climb. He then pitched forward to increase airspeed and rotor speed, but the gyroplane would still not climb. As his altitude became lower, the pilot decided to perform a forced landing to a grass area beyond the runway, rather than the harder asphalt runway. During the landing, the gyroplane landed hard, bounced, and rolled over, coming to rest on its left side.
 
The pilot further stated that he was not sure if the engine was unable to produce full power, or if he allowed the gyroplane to “fall behind the power curve” as he was also visually scanning for two airplanes in the airport traffic pattern that were utilizing runway 2.
 
Postaccident examination of the gyroplane by a Federal Aviation Administration inspector revealed substantial damage to the empennage and main rotor blades. The gyroplane’s primary flight display (PFD), engine management system (EMS), and engine control unit (ECU) were retained for data download.

Review of data downloaded from the ECU revealed that 18 minutes, 34 seconds elapsed from the time of engine start until impact. During that time, no errors, warnings, or abnormal parameters were logged that would have precluded normal operation of the engine. During climb on the accident flight, the throttle was advanced to 96.29% and the engine responded normally, reaching an rpm of 5,048.48. Just prior to the accident, the gyroplane’s descent lasted 2 minutes, 38 seconds. The pilot then reduced throttle position to 49% and the engine rpm decreased to 3,278. About 3 seconds later, the throttle position suddenly increased along with a rapid spike in engine rpm, beyond limits of 5,500, to 6,806. 

Review of data downloaded from the gyroplane’s PFD and EMS revealed that just prior to reduction in engine power for the forced landing, the engine power rpm was increasing while the rotor rpm was decreasing.

The pilot, who was also a mechanic, purchased the twin-engine airplane nearly one year prior to the accident flight. Between the time of purchase and the accident flight he had performed some maintenance of the airplane’s engines; however, the airplane had not undergone an annual inspection at any point during the preceding 15 years, nor had the pilot obtained a special flight (ferry) permit for the accident flight. Prior to departing, the pilot performed an engine runup and noted a substantial rpm drop during the right engine magneto check. He also described that he leaned both engines’ mixture controls for takeoff due to the density altitude, and because both engines would “flood out” and not run with the mixture controls in the fully forward position. During initial climb the pilot reported the airplane seemed “sluggish,” so he advanced the mixture controls forward, after which both engines lost partial power. The pilot then decreased the airplane’s pitch attitude and landed in the grass next to the runway, which resulted in substantial damage to both wings and the fuselage.
A postaccident examination of the airplane’s engines found contamination in the fuel system for the right engine. The fuel manifold valve was corroded and the fuel servo inlet screen and fuel manifold screen for the right engine were partially obstructed. Multiple spark plugs installed in the right engine exhibited corrosion, lead, and carbon fouling, and severe wear. The right engine air intake hose was found disconnected from the airbox. This condition would have likely resulted in the engine ingesting warm, unfiltered air from the cowling instead of cooler, filtered ram air. The combination of these issues likely resulted in the feeling of diminished performance the pilot reported.
The examination otherwise found no evidence of any preaccident mechanical malfunctions or failures of the left engine or the airframe that would have precluded normal operation.
Given the pilot’s statement that the engines would “flood out” and would not run with the mixture controls in the full forward position, it is likely that when the pilot advanced the mixture controls during initial climb the increased fuel flow resulted in the partial loss of power the pilot reported. Because this abnormal condition was known prior to the accident flight, the pilot should not have undertaken the flight without performing additional troubleshooting steps to fully understand and resolve the underlying issue(s).

While at OKM more maintenance was accomplished by the pilot/owner and on June 24, 2025, he flew from OKM to Fayetteville Municipal Airport (FYM), Fayetteville, Tennessee. After refueling, the pilot started both engines and reported that during the engine run-up the right engine magneto check he observed an rpm drop of about 250 rpm. Upon departure, during initial climb, the pilot reported that the airplane “seemed very sluggish.” He advanced the mixture controls for both engines forward, towards rich, after which both engines lost partial power. He decreased the airplane’s pitch attitude and attempted to land on the remaining runway. The airplane was left of the runway and touched down in the grass, which resulted in the landing gear separating and the wings impacting the ground. The impact resulted in substantial damage to both wings and the fuselage. 
A postaccident examination found that both main fuel tanks had been ruptured during the impact sequence and were absent of fuel. Both auxiliary wing fuel tanks were intact and contained liquid consistent with 100LL aviation fuel. Both fuel selectors in the cockpit were found in the off position. 
The right engine remained attached to the airplane via the engine mount. Continuity of the crankshaft, camshaft, valvetrain, and accessory case was confirmed through multiple rotations of the crankshaft. Compression and suction were observed on all cylinders. Throttle, mixture, and propeller control continuity was confirmed from the controls in the cockpit to their respective engine control attachment points and moved throughout their full range of motion. The engine air intake hose was found disconnected from the air intake box. Both magnetos remained attached and secure to the engine; they were removed and produced a spark on all leads when rotated by hand. All top spark plugs exhibited some lead and carbon fouling and rust/corrosion but retained a gap. All top sparkplugs were observed in a worn out – severe condition when compared to the Champion Aviation Check-A-Plug chart. The bottom spark plugs were examined using a lighted borescope and exhibited a worn out – severe condition when compared to the Champion Aviation Check-A-Plug chart. The nos. 1 and 3 bottom sparkplugs were lead fouled and all other bottom sparkplugs exhibited varying levels of corrosion. The fuel servo was removed, and the fuel inlet screen was removed from the servo for examination. The fuel inlet screen was partially obstructed and corroded. The fuel manifold was removed and partially disassembled to facilitate examination. The fuel manifold valve was tight and took some force to be removed, corrosion and buildup was observed on the fuel manifold valve. The fuel inlet in the manifold exhibited a large amount of corrosion and was partially obstructed. The fuel manifold screen was partially obstructed. The fuel injector lines were tight to the fuel manifold and tight on the fuel injectors. The fuel injectors were removed and were unobstructed. The oil filter was not dated; it was removed and cut open. An examination of the oil filter pleats showed no debris.
Examination of the right propeller found one blade was bent aft about 70° about 8 inches from the hub and exhibited leading edge polishing, gouges, and chordwise scratches. The other blade was bent aft about 45° about 10 inches from the hub and exhibited leading edge polishing, gouges, and chordwise scratches.
The left engine remained attached to the airplane via the engine mount. Continuity of the crankshaft, camshaft, valvetrain, and accessory case was confirmed through multiple rotations. Compression and suction were observed on all cylinders. Throttle, mixture, and propeller control continuity was confirmed from the controls in the cockpit to their respective engine control attachment points and moved throughout their full range of motion. Both magnetos remained attached and secure to the engine; they were removed and produced a spark on all leads when rotated by hand. All top sparkplugs were observed in a normal condition when compared to the Champion Aviation Check-A-Plug chart. All bottom spark plugs were examined using a lighted borescope and exhibited a worn out – normal condition when compared to the Champion Aviation Check-A-Plug chart. The fuel servo was removed, and the fuel inlet screen was removed from the servo for examination. The fuel inlet screen was unobstructed. The fuel manifold was removed and partially disassembled to facilitate examination. The fuel manifold valve was removed and was clean. The fuel manifold screen was unobstructed. The fuel injector lines were tight to the fuel manifold and tight on the fuel injectors. The fuel injectors were removed and were unobstructed. The oil filter was not dated; it was removed and cut open. An examination of the oil filter pleats showed a small amount of nonferrous debris.
Examination of the right propeller found one blade was bent aft about 45° about 12 inches from the hub. The blade exhibited leading edge polishing, leading edge gouging, and chordwise scratching. The other blade was secure in the hub and was bent aft about 70° about 12 inches from the hub. The blade exhibited leading edge polishing, leading edge gouging, and chordwise scratching.
A review of maintenance records showed the last annual inspection for the airplane was completed on February 29, 2008, at a tachometer time of 577.4 hours. The left engine was installed on the airplane after a factory overhaul on August 12, 2006, and had accumulated 87.2 hours at the time of the accident. The right engine was installed on the airplane in 1995 after a factory overhaul and had accumulated 1,389.4 hours at the time of the accident. Two entries were made on March 28, 2025, by the pilot/owner, one stated “rmvd, replaced RH engine Fuel Flow (manifold) assy” and the other stated “Removed, rebuilt, replaced fuel manifold flow divider.” An entry dated June 21, 2025. stated “removed, cleaned & reinstalled (12ea) spark plugs on LH engine upper side.” An entry from June 22, 2025, stated “Removed, cleaned & reinstalled (24ea) spark plugs on RH engine.” 
The pilot was asked if he could provide a special flight (ferry) permit under Title 14 CFR Part 21.197 and he stated, “I do not have a ferry permit to forward to you.” According to FAA airworthiness records, the owner-pilot applied for an Airworthiness Certificate replacement on November 30, 2024, but there was no record of a special flight permit request for the accident airplane.
When queried as to why the pilot had not taken off with the mixture controls set to full forward (rich) the pilot stated that he had adjusted the mixture during the engine run-up to achieve maximum rpm due to the density altitude at the airport. When asked if the engines would operate with the mixture controls in the full forward position, he reported that they would not and that they would “flood out.”
The Continental Aerospace Technologies Standard Practice Maintenance Manual (M-0) chapter 6, section 6-3 Time Between Overhaul stated:
Environmental corrosion occurs internally and externally on an engine. This naturally occurring process can affect continued airworthiness of the engine and engine mounted components or accessories. Regardless if the engine has been operated regularly or has been in storage; gaskets, seals, and synthetic and natural rubber goods deteriorate over time. Replace or overhaul the engine upon accumulating the operating hours specified in Table 6-1, or twelve (12) years after being placed in service, whichever occurs first.
The Cessna 1968 Model 310N Owner’s Manual Before Takeoff Checklist stated:
Magnetos – Check (150 RPM maximum drop with a maximum differential of 50 RPM).

On July 2, 2025, about 1729 eastern daylight time, a Cessna 208B, N716MM, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Monroe, New Jersey. The two commercial pilots and 10 passengers were seriously injured, while three passengers incurred minor injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 skydive flight.

Due to their injuries, the pilots could not initially provide a statement. According to airplane and fueling records, the accident flight was the second flight of the day. The airplane was fueled with 44.9 gallons of Jet-A, bringing the total fuel load to 800 lbs. It was then flown on an 18-minute skydive flight uneventfully. That flight departed at 1623, and the accident flight departed at 1714, with 700 lbs. of fuel onboard. 

According to preliminary ADS-B information provided by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), along with witness statements, during climb, about 3,000 ft mean sea level, the pilot reported a loss of engine power and attempted to glide the airplane back to runway 27 at Cross Keys Airport (17N), Cross, New Jersey. Runway 27 was 3,500 ft-long, 50 ft-wide, and consisted of asphalt. The airplane approached the runway fast, floated, and touched down near the end. It traveled off the end of the runway and collided with trees about 700 ft beyond the runway. It then traveled about 250 ft through the trees, coming to rest upright.

Postaccident examination of the wreckage at the accident site revealed substantial damage to the fuselage and wings. Three of the four propeller blades had separated, while the remaining blade was in a feathered position. The wreckage was subsequently recovered from the accident site and examined in further detail. Both sides of the fuselage were crushed inward. The cabin left side bench seat and right side bench seat remained intact, with the two aft legs of the left bench seat separated. The pilots’ five-point harnesses and the 17 harnesses for the bench seats in the cabin remain intact; some were cut by rescue personnel. Both wing fuel tanks and the reservoir header tank were breached; however, .5 gallon of fuel was able to be recovered from the breached reservoir header tank. The fuel was clear and absent of any visible debris. The flaps and flap jackscrew were found in the fully extended position. A multifunction display was recovered from the cockpit and retained for data download. 

A cursory examination of the (TPE331) engine was performed before it was prepared for shipment to a manufacturer facility for further teardown examination. Rotation of the propeller confirmed drivetrain continuity to the power section, gearbox scavenger pump, and accessory pad. The metal chip detector was removed, and no debris was observed. Approximately 8 ounces of fuel was drained from the fuel line to the engine fuel pump fuel filter bowl. The fuel was clear and absent of any visible debris.

On July 12, 2025, about 1322 mountain daylight time, a Piper PA-25, N8186K, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Hot Springs, South Dakota. The pilot was fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 glider aerotow flight. 
The pilot of the glider being aerotowed reported that the accident occurred during his fourth flight of the day and a pre-takeoff briefing was performed before each aerotow. The glider pilot stated that on the accident flight, after liftoff, he kept the glider in a standard tow position while he contended with updrafts until the glider reached 1,500 ft agl at which point the glider was in a higher-than-normal tow position. The glider pilot radioed the towplane pilot that he was going to release from the tow rope. The glider pilot reportedly pulled the glider’s tow rope release knob twice but did not feel the rope disconnect. He subsequently determined the glider had separated from the tow rope, and he made an otherwise uneventful landing at the airport on runway 19.
A witness reported that the towplane and glider were in a climbing left turn and were about 500 to 600 ft agl when the glider appeared to get “extremely high” on the aerotow. The towplane pitched down, and the glider appeared to release from the tow rope. According to the witness, the towplane never recovered from the nose down attitude before it impacted terrain.
The towplane impacted terrain about one mile north of the departure end of runway 6 at the Hot Springs Municipal Airport, Hot Springs, South Dakota. The towplane accident site was located on an embankment of a gravel pit, and a postaccident fire ensued. The airplane impacted terrain in an estimated 50° nose-down pitch attitude. The relative angle between the airplane at impact and the 30° sloped embankment was about 100°.  The glider tow rope with a metal ring on each end was found at the accident site. The tow rope was about 200 ft in length and was constructed of a yellow hollow braid polypropylene rope.
All primary flight control surfaces and flaps were accounted for at the accident site and remained attached to their respective attachment points. All flight control cables were found attached to their respective flight control surfaces. 
The towplane’s tow rope release latch and associated release cable were continuous from the cockpit to the latch mechanism at the tail. The latch was found in the open position, and the tow rope attachment ring was found on the ground about 15 ft from the latch. The rope extended in a south direction from the wreckage with portions suspended from tree branches. The towplane’s latch functioned normally when functionally tested.
The fixed 2-blade propeller remained attached to the engine crankshaft propeller flange. One blade exhibited an S-shaped bend and twisting near the blade tip. The leading edge exhibited leading edge polishing and chordwise scratch marks on the camber side. The other blade exhibited chordwise scratch marks on the camber side. Both blades had gouges in the leading edges. The cockpit throttle position was found to be near the idle power position, and the correlating throttle arm on the carburetor was found to be at the idle stop. The carburetor heat control arm was found in the off position. The mixture control was found in a mid-range setting. The engine crankshaft was rotated by turning the propeller by hand. No anomalies were found with the engine that would have precluded normal operation. 
The glider came to rest in the grass next to the runway. A portion of yellow rope with a metal ring attached, consistent with a “weak link” portion of a glider tow rope, was found directly under the glider. This 7 ft long section of tow rope was found with a metal ring on one end and a broom straw separation on the eye splice end, as seen in figure 1. The metal ring was found directly under the glider’s tow hook latch.

Figure 1. Broken section of glider tow rope “weak link”.
The glider was moved to a hangar for further examination. During the examination, the tow hook release knob required about 22 lbs of force to release the latching mechanism. The sound of the release cable binding in its metal conduit was heard as the release handle was moved through its full travel (forward and aft). The latch mechanism otherwise functioned normally. An exemplary glider tow hook release knob was tested and required about 4 lbs of force applied to release the latching mechanism without any audible cable binding.
The towplane was recovered from the accident site to a secure location.

On July 17, 2025, about 1122 eastern daylight time, a Piper PA-46-310P, N460WW, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Sunset, South Carolina. The commercial pilot was not injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 positioning flight.

The pilot stated that as part of his preflight inspection he added two quarts of oil to bring the engine to a total of 6.5 quarts. After departure during climb at full power the manifold pressure increased and decreased, which should have been between 35 and 36 inches of mercury (inHg). During that same time there was a corresponding exhaust gas temperature (EGT) variation. He leaned the fuel to air ratio which helped, but while over mountains he decided to continue away from them while monitoring the situation. While continuing to climb passing five or six thousand ft mean sea level (msl) the engine began vibrating with fluctuating power; the No. 2 cylinder EGT was rising and decreasing, with a corresponding engine vibration. The No. 2 cylinder head temperature (CHT) was about 100º cooler than normal, while turbo No.1 was 300 to 400° cooler; otherwise the engine gauges were in the green arc. He continued the climb then during cruise flight with the manifold pressure at 25 inHg, the No.2 cylinder EGT was reading very low 700 to 800º. Because he was above a cloud layer and unsure of the bases of the clouds due to a low instrument flight rules Airmet, he initiated a descent from 14,500 ft msl to 12,500 ft msl to not have to deal with hypoxia until he could find an area free of clouds.

After a few minutes he noted the oil pressure was at the yellow/bottom of the green arc and decided to maneuver towards Pickens County Airport (LQK), Pickens, South Carolina. The oil pressure light illuminated and with a cloud opening and the engine still developing power he reduced engine power, lowered the landing gear and after descending a few thousand ft the engine RPM increased to 3,000. He pulled the propeller control back and contacted Federal Aviation Administration air traffic control and requested to proceed direct to LQK. He then raised the landing gear and advised the controller of the situation. He slowly applied engine power, but the engine became extremely rough, and he heard a “pop” sound followed by oil spray on the windshield with smoke coming from the engine cowling. Unable to reach LQK, which was 9 to 10 nautical miles away from his present position, he decided to perform a forced landing on a golf course.

He turned back towards the golf course and applied full power but there was no change in engine rpm. He cleared trees then touched down on a golf course fairway landing up hill. After landing the main left gear separated and the nose landing gear collapsed allowing the propeller to contact the ground. After exiting the airplane he noted oil from the front of the engine cowling to the wind screen and along the length of the bottom fuselage.

Postaccident inspection of the accident site revealed that airplane came to rest about 315 ft from the initial touchdown point. A path of oil was noted exiting the right side of the nose cowling onto the windshield, and the Continental Aerospace Technologies TSIO-550-C (1) engine only had 3/4 quart of oil registering on the oil filler gauge and rod. Multiple holes were noted in the engine crankcase, the left magneto was separated, and a fractured connecting rod was observed.

The airplane was recovered and retained for further examination.

20250718200571.fa:
On July 17, 2025, about 2358 mountain daylight time, a Piper PA-28-180, N7186W, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near West Yellowstone, Montana. The pilot and two pilot rated passengers were fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight. 
The pilot and two pilot rated passengers had planned to complete a series of flights together, while two of the three pilots were building night, cross country flight time. 
According to preliminary ADS-B data provided by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the airplane landed on runway 01 at Yellowstone Airport (WYS), West Yellowstone, Montana, at 2246, and departed from runway 19 at 2353. Once airborne, the airplane’s flightpath drifted left of the runway centerline, then remained on a parallel course to the runway’s extended centerline. About 3 miles southwest of WYS, the airplane initiated a left turn to the south. About 45 seconds later, the airplane turned left to a southeasterly heading. About 28 seconds later, a right turn was initiated and continued until the end of the flight track data. No altitude information was recorded within the ADS-B data. 
According to the pilot of another airplane that landed at WYS near the time of the accident, he was inbound on an instrument flight plan and had been cleared to fly the ILS approach to runway 01 at WYS. When he was about 10 miles from WYS, he transmitted on the WYS common traffic advisory frequency (CTAF), his position and intention to fly a straight in approach to runway 01. As he completed his radio transmission, he heard a transmission from what he felt was the pilot of the accident airplane, however, it did not offer a clear description of its position. The pilot of the approaching airplane transmitted a second time and asked for position clarification from the accident pilot, who subsequently responded, “…I’m trying to get to…(garbled).” The approaching airplane’s pilot then saw aircraft lights in the distance below his airplane that were moving toward the southeast. The pilot of the approaching airplane transmitted a third time, “Are you on a left crosswind?” No further radio transmissions from the accident pilot were heard and the approaching airplane landed without further interaction with the accident pilot.
The approaching airplane’s pilot stated that at the time he flew the instrument approach into WYS, it was “very dark” and there was no landscape illumination from the moon or ground lights, other than the runway lights.
On July 18, 2025, at 1121, an Alert Notice (ALNOT) was issued following reports from family members, that the pilots could not be reached by phone, and confirmation from the airplane’s rental management company, that the airplane had not returned to its home airport. The wreckage was subsequently located by the Montana Department of Transportation Aeronautics Division, about 5.5 miles southeast of WYS, 410 ft west of the last ADS-B data point, at an elevation of about 7,580 ft msl. 
Examination of the accident site revealed that the airplane impacted wooded terrain near the top of a geographical plateau. The debris field was about 200 ft in length, from the first identified point of contact (FIPC), and was oriented on a magnetic heading of 266°. The main wreckage was located about 160 ft from the FIPC. A portion of the main wreckage came to rest in a nose low attitude, and a portion came to rest inverted. The inverted portion of the main wreckage was oriented on a magnetic heading of 299°. All major components of the airframe, flight controls, engine and propeller assembly were observed throughout the debris field.
The wreckage was recovered to a secure facility for further examination.

All Nippon Airways flight 9397, JA986A, a Boeing B787-10, collided with Breeze Airways flight 509, N247BZ, an Airbus Canada BD-500-1A11 (A220), while taxiing for takeoff at Charleston International Airport (CHS), Charleston, South Carolina. There were no crew injuries and two minor passenger injuries onboard N247BZ and no injuries to crew onboard JA986A. The left wingtip of NH9397 contacted the rudder of the N247BZ, resulting in substantial damage to both airplanes. 
Breeze Airways flight 509 was scheduled to operate from Harry Reid International Airport (LAS), Las Vegas, Nevada, to Norfolk International Airport (ORF), Norfolk, VA. Due to weather in the vicinity of ORF, the flight crew of flight 509 coordinated with the Breeze Airways dispatch team and a decision was made to divert to CHS. Dispatch coordinated with the ground service provider and CHS airport operations and was granted permission for flight 509 to park on the remain overnight (RON) ramp, spot R1, see figure 1.

 
Figure 1. Excerpt of Jeppesen 10-9 Airport Diagram Chart.
After landing, the N247BZ flight crew taxied to the RON ramp and was marshalled by ground personnel into spot R6. After shutting down the engines and starting the auxiliary power unit, the flight crew observed ground personnel approaching with air stairs and turned OFF the fasten seatbelt sign. The captain opened the cockpit door and used the public address (PA) system to inform the passengers of the plan to refuel. 
Upon returning to the cockpit, the ground personnel contacted the flight crew and stated they needed to reposition the aircraft to allow a Boeing aircraft to taxi behind them. At that time, the captain turned the seatbelt sign ON, coordinated with the flight attendants, and made a PA announcement for the passengers to return to their seats for aircraft movement. The captain kept the parking brake engaged while waiting for passengers to be seated and the ramp personnel connected the tug. At that time, the flight crew felt the aircraft suddenly and violently “jolt”. The captain queried the ground personnel and was informed that the wing of JA986A hit their tail.
JA986A was a ferry flight from CHS to Tokyo International Airport (HND), Tokyo, Japan, with a stop at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX), Los Angeles, California. The flight crew consisted of two captain qualified pilots; the pilot flying (PF) was seated in the left seat, and the pilot monitoring (PM) was seated in the right seat. The PF had operated out of CHS before, but at a different time of day. The PM had not flown out of CHS. 
The JA986A flight crew reported they received clearance to taxi to runway 15 via taxiway M. While taxiing on taxiway M, the flight crew observed good visibility but noted that it was dark and there was no taxiway centerline lighting guidance. The flight crew observed N247BZ parked ahead of them, facing West in the RON parking area (nose in), and the other airplanes were parked facing East (tail in). The flight crew assumed that the aircraft was parked for the night and was positioned in a “normal” parking spot, however as they taxied closer to the parked airplane, they thought it was “closer than normal”. 
The PF stated he was going to offset to the right, “just to be safe”. The PM indicated that he was attempting to monitor the right wing, by pressing his face against the windshield. While passing behind N247BZ, the flight crew felt a light vibration, similar to taxiing over an uneven surface. The JA986A flight crew stopped the airplane and requested airport personnel inspect their wing for potential damage, see figures 2 and 3.

Figure 2. Photograph of N247BZ (left) and JA986A (right) after the collision. (Source: Breeze Airways)

 
Figure 3. The left photo shows the damage to the vertical stabilizer and rudder of N247BZ
The right photo shows the damage to the left wing on JA986A. (Source: Breeze Airways)
JA986A sustained damage to the left raked wing tip and removable tip assembly. The removable wing tip is not considered a primary structure however the upper and lower panels of the raked wing tip are, and this damage adversely affects the structural strength requiring a major repair or replacement. Therefore, this was considered substantial damage.
Charleston Regional Aviation Authority (CRAA) provided a RON ramp parking diagram, which indicated that all odd numbered parking spots were to be tail-in parking spots and R1 was designed to hold an A220 airplane. All even spots were to be nose-in parking spots and R6 was designated for smaller airplanes. The diagram also depicts a clearance line, indicating the boundary of the ramp area and taxiway M. Photographs provided by the CRAA depicted the nose gear of N247BZ on the lead-in line to spot R6 and main landing gear beyond the clearance line, see figures 4 and 5.

Figure 4. Excerpt of CHS RON parking diagram. (Source: CRAA)

Figure 5. N247BZ nose wheel positioned prior to the RON ramp spot R6 stop bar. (Source: CRAA)
A postaccident review was conducted between Breeze Airways, CRAA, and the ground service provider. According to Breeze Airways, the ground service provider manager elected to park N247BZ on R6 due to ramp spacing for ground service equipment and the fuel truck. Additionally, they had previously parked an A220 on R6 for “gas and go” situations and had no issues. Prior to arrival, ground personnel had not cleared the ramp area of equipment and stopped the airplane with the tail beyond the ramp clearance line. Furthermore, N247BZ flight crew were unfamiliar with the RON ramp and the appropriate orientation of airplanes. They stated that the Jeppesen charts did not indicate parking directions, only spot locations. Lastly, CHS airport operations did not have prior knowledge of Boeing aircraft movements, therefore they were unaware of the potential for traffic on taxiway M.

On July 21, 2025, about 1627 eastern daylight time, a Van’s Aircraft RV-14A airplane, N21KL, was destroyed when it was involved in an accident near Lowell, Michigan. The pilot and the pilot-rated passenger sustained fatal injuries. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 91 personal flight.
The purpose of the flight was for the pilot and the passenger to view N471NP (a Van’s Aircraft RV-6 airplane), that was for sale, at the Lowell City Airport (24C), Lowell, Michigan. The passenger was interested in potentially purchasing the airplane.
A preliminary review of ADS-B data showed that the pilot departed in the airplane at 1433 from his home base at the Alpena County Regional Airport (APN), Alpena, Michigan. The airplane landed at 1456 at the Oscoda/Wurtsmith Airport (OSC), Oscoda, Michigan, and the passenger boarded the airplane. The airplane departed from OSC at 1532 and flew southwest to 24C, which is a non-towered airport.
Upon approaching 24C, the airplane flew to the west of the Flat River. The ADS-B data showed that as the airplane flew over Lincoln Lake Road, it then turned to the south. Shortly after turning south, the airplane continued in a descending turn toward the east. The airplane impacted a storage unit building about 0.43 miles from the approach end of runway 12 at 24C.
When the airplane impacted the storage unit building, an explosion occurred. A postimpact fire consumed the wreckage and the storage unit building. The wreckage was recovered from the accident site, and it was transported to a secure location.
According to a witness, he and his son observed the airplane inflight while they were driving in a vehicle near 24C on Vergennes Street. While the airplane was in the descending turn and prior to impact, they did not observe any smoke or flames emitting from the airplane, nor did they hear any abnormal engine noises such as sputtering or backfiring.
The two-seat experimental airplane was built from a kit in 2024 by the pilot, who in addition to holding a private pilot certificate (airplane single engine land), he also held a repairman certificate (experimental aircraft builder for the accident airplane). The passenger held a private pilot certificate (airplane single engine land) and an airframe and powerplant mechanic certificate.
The airplane was equipped with a Lycoming Engines YIO-390-EXP248 reciprocating engine, part of the Thunderbolt experimental engine series. The airplane was also equipped with a Whirlwind Propellers 300-3B/A-72 three-blade controllable pitch composite propeller.
A preliminary review of meteorological data for the accident location and time did not reveal any meteorological areas of concern. The calculated density altitude for the closest meteorological reporting station was 2,266 ft.

20250722200603.fa:
On July 22, 2025, about 0930 central daylight time, a Cessna T188C, N2802J, was substantially damaged when it was involved in an accident near Oregon, Illinois. The pilot was fatally injured. The airplane was operated as a Title 14 Code of Federal Regulations Part 137 aerial application flight.
A company responsible for delivering and loading agricultural chemicals was loading the airplanes for the operator. According to the loader, the pilot arrived at the Ogle County Airport (C55), Mount Morris, Illinois about 0600 to start his workday. He completed five flights to a field about 5 miles northeast of C55 and upon returning to the airport, the pilot reported having an issue with the product dispersal system. The ground crew cleaned the spraybar screen while the airplane was idling. The pilot requested a partial load of chemical so that in the event the dispersal system did not function properly, he would not land with a heavy load. The loader filled the liquid chemical hopper with the requested amount, and the pilot departed about 0930. 
Multiple witnesses reported seeing the accident airplane in a “hard” left bank just over the top of standing corn, which stood about 8 ft tall. One witness reported that the airplane struck the powerline, impacted the ground nose first, bounced and immediately was engulfed in flames. The airplane skidded across a road and came to rest about 100 ft north of the initial impact point at the edge of a corn field. Cut powerlines were observed about 685 ft north of the departure end of runway 09 and portions were laid across the road. A utility pole was fractured and leaning in a north direction. A post-impact fire ensued.
The airplane came to rest on its left side on about a 300° heading. Ground scars included blue paint transfer and a cut in the asphalt road about 2.5 in. deep, consistent with propeller blade contact. All structural components and flight control surfaces were located at the accident site. The left elevator balance horn displayed evidence of scoring from the asphalt surface of the road. A 12 – 18 in. section of the outboard leading edge of the right wing, including part of the outboard rib and composite wing tip was found near a section of cut powerlines about 100 ft south of the main wreckage and had witness marks consistent with a wire strike. The remaining portion of the right wing leading edge was thermally damaged. None of the installed wire cutters displayed evidence of wire strikes or arcing. 
Flight control cable continuity was established from the ailerons, elevators and rudder to the cockpit controls. The elevator trim control cable continuity was established from the trim tab to the forward chain in the cockpit that separated from the sprocket due to thermal damage. Flap control continuity was established from the flap handle to the pushrod attach structure on each flap. The flap handle position was found at full extension, however the actual flap position at the time of the accident could not be determined.
The cockpit and inboard wing sections were thermally damaged. The cockpit and instrument panel were thermally damaged in the post impact fire.
The emergency dump gate of the product dispersal system was thermally damaged. The gate door was thermally separated from its mounts; however, the hinges and door attach points were found in the closed position.
The fuel system was thermally damaged and could not be tested. The fuel strainer and header tank were not observed in the wreckage. Both wing tanks were ruptured, and any remaining fuel was consumed by fire.
A cursory examination of the engine was performed. The engine had been exposed to thermal damage. The top spark plugs were removed; the No. 2, 4, and 6 spark plugs were covered in oil due to the position of the engine. The plug electrodes were consistent with “worn out – normal” when compared to a Champion inspection chart. The fuel pump was removed and was unremarkable; the pump drive shaft was intact. The engine crankshaft was turned through by manually rotating the propeller which remained attached to the crankshaft; suction and compression were observed on all cylinders, and no internal binding was observed. Both magnetos remained attached to the engine. No spark was observed, however both magnetos had been exposed to thermal forces. The engine controls remained attached to the fuel control.
A borescope examination of the cylinders, piston faces, valves and lower sparkplugs found no anomalies. 
The oil filter was removed and cut. The filter media was brittle and charred due to thermal forces, however no contaminants or particles were found.
All three propeller blades exhibited bending, curling, and chord-wise scratches. Two blades exhibited S bending, and one blade had 8 in. of the tip bent back on itself with a fracture at the bend. The retaining rings for all three blades separated and two of the blades rotated freely in the hub.
The airplane was recovered to a secure facility for future examination.

20250723200619.an:
On arrival at Santa Barbara Municipal Airport (SBA), Santa Barbara, California, United Airlines flight 2428 (UAL2428), operating from San Francisco International Airport (SFO), San Francisco, California, experienced multiple electrical system fault indications after landing and during taxi-in. Following the aircraft’s arrival at its gate, a ramp service agent sustained serious injuries after entering the jet blast area of an engine that remained running during ramp operations. No damage to the aircraft was reported.

The flight crew reported that the flight segment from SFO to SBA was uneventful. After landing and clearing the runway, the first officer (FO), who was the pilot monitoring, started the auxiliary power unit (APU) and conducted the after-landing checklist. The captain, who was the pilot flying, taxied the airplane toward gate 2, where ramp personnel were positioned to receive the aircraft.

As the airplane approached the stopping point at the gate, the Electronic Centralized Aircraft Monitoring (ECAM) system annunciated a Level 2 caution chime and light with a “ELEC APU GEN FAULT” on the Engine/Warning Display. The captain verbalized “ECAM” and instructed the FO to “Stand by” on the ECAM procedure as the captain prioritized their parking guidance. Upon reaching the designated gate stop point, the marshaller signaled the flight crew to stop the airplane, and the captain set the parking brake. The FO subsequently shut down the Number 2 (right) engine in accordance with the standard parking procedure.

Immediately following the right engine shutdown, the flight crew observed multiple ECAM fault messages, including an intermittent right engine fire warning accompanied by an aural alert and illumination of associated warning lights. The indication cleared within several seconds. With the left engine still running and the aircraft beacon still on the captain instructed the FO to begin ECAM actions to try and get the APU GEN back online. The flight crew attempted to reset the APU generator; however, the fault condition persisted. The crew then requested ground power before shutting down the remaining Number 1 (left) engine. Ramp personnel informed the crew that jet bridge power could not be connected while the left engine was still operating. A portable ground power unit (GPU) was subsequently retrieved and connected to the aircraft. After verifying that external power was available, the flight crew shut down the left engine and completed the parking checklist. According to the captain, the elapsed time from parking brake set to engine shutdown was approximately 10 minutes.

Once the aircraft was secured, the captain and FO coordinated with United Maintenance Control to troubleshoot the electrical system faults. During this time, the FO was informed by the ramp lead that one of the ground crew members, serving as a wing walker, had sustained a serious injury from jet blast while the left engine remained running. According to the ramp lead, the injured wing walker approached the aircraft prematurely to place chalks at the main landing gear and entered the jet blast zone without confirming that the left engine had been shut down. The ramp lead indicated that the employee was relatively new and may have misinterpreted marshalling procedures, potentially confusing the procedures with those used by other carriers operating at SBA.

According to United, there were 5 ground crew members in place to bring in UAL2428. The marshaller was behind the aircraft nose stop mark, one wing walker was on the left-wing side of the airplane, the lead ramp agent and the right-wing walker was at the right-wing side of the airplane, and another support ramp agent was by the jetbridge to handle the chocks and other arrival duties. Once the aircraft came to a stop, the marshaller gave the X signal (stop), and the support agent placed the nose landing gear chocks. 

The support ramp agent does not need an all-clear signal to chock the nose landing gear, as this position is not exposed to engine jet blast. The marshaller then gave the hand signal to the flight crew indicating that the aircraft was chocked and lowered his hands. Standard procedure requires the left and right wing walkers—who are potentially exposed to engine jet blast—to wait for an all-clear signal from the marshaller before approaching the airplane to chock the main landing gear.

The injured ramp service agent (left wing walker) indicated that he was waiting for the “safe-to-approach” signal from the marshaller but was uncertain whether he misinterpreted the signal or received it in error. He proceeded behind the left engine while carrying wheel chocks, unaware that the engine was still operating. He recalled being struck by jet blast and falling onto his left side, sustaining multiple injuries. He reported experiencing shock and was unable to feel pain immediately after impact. Nearby personnel assisted him and transported him to the on-site emergency response vehicle. The injured agent reported that he was not distracted or under time pressure and had already serviced four flights that day. 

The lead ramp agent stated that the ramp experienced a brief delay due to the ongoing electrical issue reported by the flight crew. During this time, the injured ramp agent appeared to misinterpret the marshaller’s gestures as the all-clear signal and began approaching the aircraft carrying two wheel chocks. The lead agent observed that the anti-collision beacon remained illuminated and that the left engine was still operating. He attempted to radio the injured agent to stop, but the agent did not appear to have heard the transmission. Moments later, the agent was struck by the exhaust blast from the operating left engine resulting in the agent being thrown to the ground.

Following the accident, United issued a safety alert reminding the employees that aircraft must only be approached after marshallers give the “Safe to Approach” signal and only after confirming the nose gear is chocked, both engines are fully shut down and spooled down, the beacon light is off, and emphasizing “when in doubt, wait.”

Endeavor Air flight 4985 encountered severe turbulence while descending through 17,400 feet to Cincinnati Northern Kentucky International Airport (CVG), after which a passenger reported a serious injury after seeking follow-up medical care. 
The flight crew reported that the fasten seat belt sign was illuminated, and a public address (PA) announcement had been made instructing passengers to fasten their seat belts and remain seated. As the aircraft descended through about 17,400 feet, the pilots observed a cumulus cloud directly ahead that had not been displayed on the airplane’s weather radar as moderate or severe returns. The captain reduced the descent rate and continued through the top of the cloud, when the aircraft encountered severe turbulence.
At the time of the turbulence encounter, the two flight attendants (FAs) were conducting final cabin safety checks. During the event, both FAs were lifted into the air and thrown to the floor, with one FA striking their head on the ceiling of the aircraft. 
Following the turbulence, both FAs returned to their assigned jump seats and secured their safety harnesses, while checking on passengers. A public address (PA) announcement was made instructing passengers to “please take your seat and fasten your seatbelt,” followed by a second announcement advising passengers to press their call button if they required assistance.
Two passengers activated their call buttons and reported striking their heads on the ceiling during the turbulence encounter. Upon arrival at the gate, medical personnel met the aircraft. After evaluation, both passengers were released.
Endeavor Air received an unverified report following the flight that one passenger sought further medical treatment and was subsequently diagnosed with a serious injury. 
At the time of the turbulence encounter there was no active significant meteorological information (SIGMETs), convective SIGMETs, airman’s meteorological information (AIRMETs), or pilot reports (PIREPs) of any significant turbulence.
